claim: Platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (Pdgfra) is required for cardiac fusion.
source: We previously showed however, that the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (Pdgfra) is also required for cardiac fusion (Bloomekatz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Bloomekatz et al., 2017).

claim: The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) intracellular signaling pathway has an essential intrinsic role in the myocardium directing movement toward the midline.
source: Here, we show that the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) intracellular signaling pathway has an essential intrinsic role in the myocardium directing movement toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including pharmacological inhibition and genetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions become unpolarized in PI3K-inhibited zebrafish embryos.
source: In vivo imaging further reveals midline-oriented dynamic myocardial membrane protrusions that become unpolarized in PI3K-inhibited zebrafish embryos where myocardial movements are misdirected and slower.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myocardial movements are misdirected and slower in PI3K-inhibited zebrafish embryos.
source: In vivo imaging further reveals midline-oriented dynamic myocardial membrane protrusions that become unpolarized in PI3K-inhibited zebrafish embryos where myocardial movements are misdirected and slower.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data and quantitative analysis of cell movements.

claim: PI3K activity is dependent on Pdgfra.
source: Moreover, we find that PI3K activity is dependent on and interacts with Pdgfra to regulate myocardial movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced PI3K activity in pdgfra mutants and genetic interaction studies.

claim: PI3K interacts with Pdgfra to regulate myocardial movement.
source: Moreover, we find that PI3K activity is dependent on and interacts with Pdgfra to regulate myocardial movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing synergistic effects.

claim: Bilateral myocardial precursors collectively move toward the midline (cardiac fusion) to form the primitive heart tube during heart development.
source: During heart development, bilateral myocardial precursors collectively move toward the midline (cardiac fusion) to form the primitive heart tube.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cardiac development.

claim: The adjacent anterior endoderm is required for cardiac fusion.
source: Extrinsic influences such as the adjacent anterior endoderm are known to be required for cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Myocardial cells are specified bilaterally on either side of the embryo.
source: Progenitor cell movement occurs during cardiac development, where myocardial cells are specified bilaterally on either side of the embryo (Stainier et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Stainier et al., 1993).

claim: Myocardial cells undergo a mesenchymal-to-epithelial (MET) transition forming intercellular junctions during cardiac fusion.
source: As they move, myocardial cells undergo a mesenchymal-to-epithelial (MET) transition forming intercellular junctions and subsequently moving together as an epithelial collective (Trinh and Stainier, 2004; Jackson et al., 2017; Dominguez et al., 2023; Linask, 1992; Holtzman et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cardiac fusion occurs in all vertebrates.
source: This process is known as cardiac fusion and occurs in all vertebrates (Davidson et al., 2005; Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in zebrafish and mice which inhibit endoderm specification or disrupt endoderm morphogenesis result in cardia bifida.
source: Mutations in zebrafish and mice which inhibit endoderm specification or disrupt endoderm morphogenesis result in cardia bifida – a phenotype in which the bilateral myocardial populations fail to merge (Holtzman et al., 2007; Alexander et al., 1999; Kupperman et al., 2000; Osborne et al., 2008; Kawahara et al., 2009; Kikuchi et al., 2001; Mendelson et al., 2015; Molkentin et al., 1997; Ye and Lin, 2013; Li et al., 2004; Yelon et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cardia bifida is a phenotype in which the bilateral myocardial populations fail to merge.
source: Mutations in zebrafish and mice which inhibit endoderm specification or disrupt endoderm morphogenesis result in cardia bifida – a phenotype in which the bilateral myocardial populations fail to merge (Holtzman et al., 2007; Alexander et al., 1999; Kupperman et al., 2000; Osborne et al., 2008; Kawahara et al., 2009; Kikuchi et al., 2001; Mendelson et al., 2015; Molkentin et al., 1997; Ye and Lin, 2013; Li et al., 2004; Yelon et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Mechanical disruption of the endoderm in chicks and rats results in cardiac fusion phenotypes similar to cardia bifida.
source: Similar phenotypes also occur in chicks and rats when the endoderm is mechanically disrupted (Goss, 1935; Rosenquist, 1970; Varner and Taber, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is a correlation between the movements of the endoderm and myocardium during cardiac fusion.
source: Studies simultaneously observing endoderm and myocardial movement have found a correlation between the movements of these two tissues, suggesting a model in which the endoderm provides the mechanical force that pulls myocardial cells toward the midline (Varner and Taber, 2012; Cui et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2015; Aleksandrova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The endoderm provides the mechanical force that pulls myocardial cells toward the midline.
source: Studies simultaneously observing endoderm and myocardial movement have found a correlation between the movements of these two tissues, suggesting a model in which the endoderm provides the mechanical force that pulls myocardial cells toward the midline (Varner and Taber, 2012; Cui et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2015; Aleksandrova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is presented as a suggested model based on correlations observed in cited studies.

claim: Correlations between endoderm and myocardial movement do not occur at all stages of cardiac fusion.
source: Yet, these correlations do not occur at all stages of cardiac fusion, indicating that myocardial cells may also use intrinsic mechanisms to actively move toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from prior studies and leads to an inference about intrinsic mechanisms.

claim: Myocardial cells may use intrinsic mechanisms to actively move toward the midline.
source: Yet, these correlations do not occur at all stages of cardiac fusion, indicating that myocardial cells may also use intrinsic mechanisms to actively move toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that correlations do not occur at all stages.

claim: Pdgfra has a role in the movement of myocardial cells.
source: Indeed, recent studies revealing a role for the receptor tyrosine kinase, platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (Pdgfra) in the movement of myocardial cells have suggested a paracrine chemotaxis model, in which the myocardium senses chemokine signals from the endoderm and responds to them (Bloomekatz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Bloomekatz et al., 2017).

claim: A paracrine chemotaxis model has been suggested in which the myocardium senses chemokine signals from the endoderm and responds to them.
source: Indeed, recent studies revealing a role for the receptor tyrosine kinase, platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (Pdgfra) in the movement of myocardial cells have suggested a paracrine chemotaxis model, in which the myocardium senses chemokine signals from the endoderm and responds to them (Bloomekatz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is presented as a suggested model based on cited work.

claim: The PI3K pathway is an intracellular signaling mediator of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs; e.g. Pdgfra).
source: The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is known as an intracellular signaling mediator of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs; e.g. Pdgfra).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about PI3K signaling.

claim: During PI3K signaling, PI3K phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to create phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3).
source: During PI3K signaling, PI3K phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to create phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3), which recruits pleckstrin homology (PH)-domain containing proteins and regulates many cellular processes including proliferation and cell migration (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: PIP3 recruits pleckstrin homology (PH)-domain containing proteins.
source: During PI3K signaling, PI3K phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to create phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3), which recruits pleckstrin homology (PH)-domain containing proteins and regulates many cellular processes including proliferation and cell migration (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: PI3K signaling regulates many cellular processes including proliferation and cell migration.
source: During PI3K signaling, PI3K phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) to create phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3), which recruits pleckstrin homology (PH)-domain containing proteins and regulates many cellular processes including proliferation and cell migration (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: PI3K signaling regulates individualistic cell migration in Dictyostelium and neutrophils.
source: Both individualistic cell migration such as in Dictyostelium and neutrophils (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010) and collective cell migration such as in the movement of border cells in Drosophila and the movement of the anterior visceral endoderm during mouse gastrulation (Ghiglione et al., 2018; Bloomekatz et al., 2012) have been shown to be regulated by PI3K signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010).

claim: PI3K signaling regulates collective cell migration in border cells in Drosophila.
source: Both individualistic cell migration such as in Dictyostelium and neutrophils (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010) and collective cell migration such as in the movement of border cells in Drosophila and the movement of the anterior visceral endoderm during mouse gastrulation (Ghiglione et al., 2018; Bloomekatz et al., 2012) have been shown to be regulated by PI3K signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Ghiglione et al., 2018).

claim: PI3K signaling regulates the movement of the anterior visceral endoderm during mouse gastrulation.
source: Both individualistic cell migration such as in Dictyostelium and neutrophils (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010) and collective cell migration such as in the movement of border cells in Drosophila and the movement of the anterior visceral endoderm during mouse gastrulation (Ghiglione et al., 2018; Bloomekatz et al., 2012) have been shown to be regulated by PI3K signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Bloomekatz et al., 2012).

claim: Inhibition of the PI3K pathway results in bilateral cardiomyocyte populations that fail to reach the midline (cardia bifida) or have only partially merged by the time wild-type myocardial cells are fully merged.
source: In particular, we find that inhibition of the PI3K pathway, throughout the embryo or only in the myocardium, results in bilateral cardiomyocyte populations that fail to reach the midline (cardia bifida) or have only partially merged by the time wild-type myocardial cells are fully merged.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The orientation of myocardial membrane protrusions during cardiac fusion is dependent on PI3K signaling.
source: High-resolution live imaging in combination with mosaic labeling further reveals that the orientation of myocardial membrane protrusions during cardiac fusion is dependent on PI3K signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution live imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PI3K and Pdgfra interact to facilitate cardiac fusion.
source: Furthermore, we find that PI3K and Pdgfra interact to facilitate cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsic Pdgfra–PI3K signaling regulates the formation of membrane protrusions, facilitating the collective movement of the myocardium toward the midline.
source: Altogether our work supports a model by which intrinsic Pdgfra–PI3K signaling regulates the formation of membrane protrusions, facilitating the collective movement of the myocardium toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is a model supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In wild-type or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated embryos, bilateral myocardial populations move toward the midline and merge to form a ring structure between 20 and 21 hpf, which corresponds to the 20–22 somite stage (s).
source: In wild-type or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated embryos, bilateral myocardial populations move toward the midline and merge to form a ring structure between 20 and 21 hpf, which corresponds to the 20–22 somite stage (s) (Figure 1A, A', F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, A', F, G.

claim: In embryos treated with 15–25 μM LY myocardial movement is disrupted and the bilateral myocardial populations fail to properly merge by 22s.
source: However, in embryos treated with 15–25 μM LY myocardial movement is disrupted and the bilateral myocardial populations fail to properly merge by 22s (Figure 1B, B', F, G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C, M).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, B', F, G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C, M.

claim: Exposure to PI3K inhibitors Dactolisib (Dac) or Pictilisib (Pic) (20–50 μM) causes cardiac fusion defects.
source: Exposure to these PI3K inhibitors (20–50 μM) causes cardiac fusion defects (Figure 1A–D, A'–D', F, G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I, N, O) and corresponding reductions in PI3K activity, as measured by the ratio of phosphorylated AKT (pAKT) to AKT (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Exposure to PI3K inhibitors Dactolisib (Dac) or Pictilisib (Pic) (20–50 μM) causes corresponding reductions in PI3K activity, as measured by the ratio of phosphorylated AKT (pAKT) to AKT.
source: Exposure to these PI3K inhibitors (20–50 μM) causes cardiac fusion defects (Figure 1A–D, A'–D', F, G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I, N, O) and corresponding reductions in PI3K activity, as measured by the ratio of phosphorylated AKT (pAKT) to AKT (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q–R.

claim: AKT is phosphorylated as a direct consequence of PI3K activity.
source: AKT is phosphorylated as a direct consequence of PI3K activity (Alessi et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: Incubating embryos from bud stage to 22s with rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR, at multiple concentrations did not affect cardiac fusion.
source: Incubating embryos from bud stage to 22s with rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR (Heitman et al., 1991), at multiple concentrations did not affect cardiac fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F), even though mTOR activity as measured by S6 phosphorylation (Holz and Blenis, 2005) was dramatically reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F.

claim: mTOR activity as measured by S6 phosphorylation was dramatically reduced in rapamycin-treated embryos.
source: Incubating embryos from bud stage to 22s with rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR (Heitman et al., 1991), at multiple concentrations did not affect cardiac fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F), even though mTOR activity as measured by S6 phosphorylation (Holz and Blenis, 2005) was dramatically reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: mRNA injection of a truncated form of p85, which acts as a dominant negative inhibitor of PI3K (dnPI3K) activity, caused cardiac fusion defects.
source: Furthermore, using a non-pharmacological approach we found that mRNA injection of a truncated form of p85, which acts as a dominant negative inhibitor of PI3K (dnPI3K) activity (Carballada et al., 2001) also caused cardiac fusion defects (Figure 1E, E', F, G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–L, P, S).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figures and by a citation describing the dominant negative construct.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K activity with LY, Dac, Pic, and dominant-negative p85 mRNA, but not mTOR causes cardiac fusion defects.
source: Thus, inhibition of PI3K activity with LY, Dac, Pic, and dominant-negative p85 mRNA, but not mTOR causes cardiac fusion defects.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: During the later stages of cardiac fusion, myocardial cells develop epithelial polarity in which proteins such as ZO1 form intercellular junctions between myocardial cells.
source: During the later stages of cardiac fusion, myocardial cells develop epithelial polarity in which proteins such as ZO1 form intercellular junctions between myocardial cells (Trinh and Stainier, 2004; Jackson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and is supported by citations.

claim: During cardiac fusion, the myocardium moves deeper into the tissue eventually residing ventral to the endoderm in a process known as subduction.
source: During this time, the myocardium also moves deeper into the tissue eventually residing ventral to the endoderm in a process known as subduction (Ye et al., 2015) and it forms a contiguous second dorsal layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C, arrows).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by a citation and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: The myocardium forms a contiguous second dorsal layer during cardiac fusion.
source: During this time, the myocardium also moves deeper into the tissue eventually residing ventral to the endoderm in a process known as subduction (Ye et al., 2015) and it forms a contiguous second dorsal layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: In PI3K-inhibited embryos, myocardial cells form a second dorsal layer.
source: In PI3K-inhibited embryos, we found that myocardial cells form this second dorsal layer however, the localization of polarity markers and the tissue organization can appear mildly disorganized (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F.

claim: The localization of polarity markers and the tissue organization can appear mildly disorganized in PI3K-inhibited embryos.
source: In PI3K-inhibited embryos, we found that myocardial cells form this second dorsal layer however, the localization of polarity markers and the tissue organization can appear mildly disorganized (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–F.

claim: The PI3K signaling pathway is known to promote cell proliferation and cell survival.
source: The PI3K signaling pathway is known to promote cell proliferation and cell survival (Fruman et al., 2017) however, we did not find a difference in the number of cardiomyocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G–I) nor in the number of cardiomyocytes in S-phase as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4J–L) in PI3K-inhibited embryos at 20s compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: There was no difference in the number of cardiomyocytes in PI3K-inhibited embryos at 20s compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
source: The PI3K signaling pathway is known to promote cell proliferation and cell survival (Fruman et al., 2017) however, we did not find a difference in the number of cardiomyocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G–I) nor in the number of cardiomyocytes in S-phase as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4J–L) in PI3K-inhibited embryos at 20s compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4G–I.

claim: There was no difference in the number of cardiomyocytes in S-phase as measured by EdU incorporation in PI3K-inhibited embryos at 20s compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
source: The PI3K signaling pathway is known to promote cell proliferation and cell survival (Fruman et al., 2017) however, we did not find a difference in the number of cardiomyocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G–I) nor in the number of cardiomyocytes in S-phase as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4J–L) in PI3K-inhibited embryos at 20s compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4J–L.

claim: No apoptotic cardiomyocytes were observed in DMSO- nor in 20 μM LY-treated embryos.
source: Similarly, no apoptotic cardiomyocytes were observed in DMSO- nor in 20 μM LY-treated embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 4M–P, n = 17, 19 embryos, respectively, from three biological replicates), despite apoptosis being observed in DNAse-treated controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4O, P).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4M–P.

claim: Pten, a lipid phosphatase, opposes PI3K function by converting PIP3 to PIP2.
source: Pten, a lipid phosphatase, opposes PI3K function by converting PIP3 to PIP2 (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: Homozygous ptena−/− mutants, along with double homozygous ptena−/−, ptenb−/− mutants did not show defects in cardiac fusion.
source: Homozygous ptena−/− mutants, along with double homozygous ptena−/−, ptenb−/− mutants did not show defects in cardiac fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C, J.

claim: Maternal contribution of Pten has been reported to persist till at least 60 hpf.
source: However, maternal contribution of Pten has been reported to persist till at least 60 hpf (Choorapoikayil et al., 2013; Faucherre et al., 2008), possibly explaining the lack of phenotype in these mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cardiac fusion defects have been observed in pten mutant mouse embryos.
source: Indeed, cardiac fusion defects have been observed in pten mutant mouse embryos (Bloomekatz et al., 2012) and we found that inhibiting Pten in zebrafish embryos from bud stage to 22s with the small molecule Pten inhibitor VO-OHpic (Rosivatz et al., 2006) does result in cardiac fusion defects, along with increased PI3K activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Bloomekatz et al., 2012).

claim: Inhibiting Pten in zebrafish embryos from bud stage to 22s with the small molecule Pten inhibitor VO-OHpic results in cardiac fusion defects, along with increased PI3K activity.
source: Indeed, cardiac fusion defects have been observed in pten mutant mouse embryos (Bloomekatz et al., 2012) and we found that inhibiting Pten in zebrafish embryos from bud stage to 22s with the small molecule Pten inhibitor VO-OHpic (Rosivatz et al., 2006) does result in cardiac fusion defects, along with increased PI3K activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Adding a sub-phenotypic dose of VO-OHpic to double homozygous ptena−/−, ptenb−/− mutant embryos results in cardiac fusion defects.
source: Furthermore, adding a sub-phenotypic dose of VO-OHpic (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D–F) to double homozygous ptena−/−, ptenb−/− mutant embryos to address the role of the remaining maternal contribution also results in cardiac fusion defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G–J, Fisher's test p-value 8.21E−06).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5G–J with statistical analysis.

claim: Appropriate levels of PI3K signaling are required for proper cardiac fusion.
source: These findings reveal that loss-of-Pten which causes increased PIP3 levels results in cardiac fusion defects and together with our PI3K inhibition experiments indicate that appropriate levels of PI3K signaling are required for proper cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing both loss and gain of PI3K activity cause defects.

claim: PI3K-inhibited embryos display cardiac phenotypes at 22s that range from severe cardia bifida to more mildly affected hearts in which the myocardial populations form a U-shaped structure.
source: PI3K-inhibited embryos display cardiac phenotypes at 22s that range from severe, in which the myocardial populations remain entirely separate (cardia bifida) (Figure 1G – red; examples – Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, F, I, L), to more mildly affected hearts in which the myocardial populations form a U-shaped structure, having merged at the posterior but not anterior end (Figure 1G – orange; examples Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, E, H, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of the PI3K-inhibited embryos appear phenotypically normal (~25% for 20 μM LY) indicating incomplete penetrance.
source: A subset of the PI3K-inhibited embryos also appear phenotypically normal (~25% for 20 μM LY, Figure 1F, G) indicating incomplete penetrance.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F, G.

claim: Increasing the concentration of PI3K inhibitor or dnPI3K mRNA increases the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion phenotypes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: However, increasing the concentration of PI3K inhibitor or dnPI3K mRNA increases the severity and penetrance of these phenotypes in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LY inhibits PI3K activity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Similarly, we confirmed that LY inhibits PI3K activity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion defects depend on the efficacy of PI3K inhibition.
source: Thus, the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion defects depend on the efficacy of PI3K inhibition.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the dose-dependent effects observed.

claim: Differing modes of movement and cellular processes such as MET and subduction occur at distinct developmental stages during cardiac fusion.
source: Since differing modes of movement (Holtzman et al., 2007) and cellular processes such as MET (Trinh and Stainier, 2004; Jackson et al., 2017) and subduction (Ye et al., 2015) occur at distinct developmental stages during cardiac fusion, we evaluated the developmental stages over which PI3K signaling is required.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Short exposures (<3 hr) of LY just prior to 22s or starting at bud stage had no effect on cardiac fusion.
source: Short exposures (<3 hr) just prior to 22s or starting at bud stage had no effect on cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from addition and wash-out experiments.

claim: Progressively longer times of exposure to LY ending at 22s or starting at bud stage result in correspondingly more severe phenotypes and higher penetrance.
source: However, progressively longer times of exposure ending at 22s or starting at bud stage result in correspondingly more severe phenotypes and higher penetrance (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Both the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion phenotypes correlate with the duration of LY incubation and not a specific developmental stage inside the 3–20s window.
source: These addition and wash-out experiments indicate that both the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion phenotypes correlate with the duration of LY incubation and not a specific developmental stage inside the 3–20s window.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the addition and wash-out experimental data.

claim: The translocation of the myocardium toward the midline is responsive to both the levels and duration of PI3K signaling throughout cardiac fusion.
source: Thus, the translocation of the myocardium toward the midline is responsive to both the levels and duration of PI3K signaling throughout cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the dose-dependent and time-dependent effects observed.

claim: When PI3K signaling is inhibited with 15 or 25 μM LY starting at bud stage, no differences were observed in the expression of endoderm markers such as axial/foxa2 or Tg(sox17:egfp) compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
source: However, when PI3K signaling is inhibited with 15 or 25 μM LY starting at bud stage we did not observe differences in the expression of endoderm markers such as axial/foxa2 or Tg(sox17:egfp) compared to DMSO-treated embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, E–G.

claim: The anterior endoderm morphology in PI3K-inhibited embryos was intact and contiguous similar to DMSO-treated embryos.
source: A detailed examination of the anterior endoderm morphology in PI3K-inhibited embryos revealed it was intact and contiguous similar to DMSO-treated embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, J) as was the average anterior endoderm width (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, J, D, H.

claim: Cardiac fusion defects in PI3K-inhibited embryos are unlikely to be due to changes in the anterior endoderm.
source: Thus, cardiac fusion defects in PI3K-inhibited embryos are unlikely to be due to changes in the anterior endoderm.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that the endoderm appears normal in PI3K-inhibited embryos.

claim: In F1 embryos at 22s derived from incrosses between Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) mosaic F0 animals, embryos with normal cardiac rings did not have the transgene (n = 71/71).
source: Genotyping revealed that F1 embryos with normal cardiac rings (Figure 2D–G) did not have the transgene (n = 71/71), while almost all sibling embryos with cardiac fusion defects (Figure 2D'–G') were positive for the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene (n = 43/44).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data and images shown in Figure 2D–G.

claim: Almost all F1 sibling embryos with cardiac fusion defects were positive for the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene (n = 43/44).
source: Genotyping revealed that F1 embryos with normal cardiac rings (Figure 2D–G) did not have the transgene (n = 71/71), while almost all sibling embryos with cardiac fusion defects (Figure 2D'–G') were positive for the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene (n = 43/44).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data and images shown in Figure 2D'–G'.

claim: All embryos with the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene have a cardiac fusion defect.
source: And all embryos with the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene have a cardiac fusion defect (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene is significantly associated with a cardiac fusion defect (Fisher's test p = 5.56 × 10−31).
source: Statistical analysis reveals that the Tg(myl7:dnPI3K) transgene is significantly associated with a cardiac fusion defect (Fisher's test p = 5.56 × 10−31).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the genotyping and phenotyping data.

claim: PI3K signaling is active in the myocardium during cardiac fusion.
source: We further confirmed that PI3K signaling is active in the myocardium during cardiac fusion by using a PH domain reporter (Balla and Várnai, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by PH domain reporter data.

claim: Fluorophores fused to PH-domains from PIP3-binding proteins translocate to the membrane when PIP3 is induced.
source: Fluorophores fused to PH-domains from PIP3-binding proteins translocate to the membrane when PIP3 is induced.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PH domain reporters.

claim: The PH-domain from BTK fused to mkate2 localizes to the region of the plasma membrane where PI3K is actively creating PIP3.
source: For example, the PH-domain from BTK fused to mkate2 localizes to the region of the plasma membrane where PI3K is actively creating PIP3 (Hall et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Hall et al., 2020).

claim: PH-mkate2 was enriched asymmetrically at intercellular plasma membrane boundaries in DMSO-treated embryos at 20s.
source: By expressing this reporter (myl7:PH-mkate2) mosaically in the myocardium, we found that PH-mkate2 was enriched asymmetrically at intercellular plasma membrane boundaries in DMSO-treated embryos at 20s (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–A''', C–E, Figure 2—video 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–A''', C–E.

claim: In PI3K-inhibited embryos PH-mkate2 was localized diffusely throughout the cytoplasm or in subcellular compartments.
source: However, in PI3K-inhibited embryos PH-mkate2 was localized diffusely throughout the cytoplasm or in subcellular compartments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E, Figure 2—video 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: PI3K signaling acts within the myocardium to regulate its movement during cardiac fusion.
source: Combined with our tissue-specific inhibition of PI3K signaling these findings suggest that PI3K signaling acts within the myocardium to regulate its movement during cardiac fusion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the tissue-specific inhibition and PH domain reporter data.

claim: A time-series using hand2 expression reveals dramatic differences between DMSO- and LY-treated embryos in the translocation of the myocardium beginning after 12s.
source: A time-series using hand2 expression reveals dramatic differences between DMSO- and LY-treated embryos in the translocation of the myocardium beginning after 12s (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In time-lapse movies of DMSO-treated embryos, myocardial cells display coherent medially directed movement with an average velocity of 0.2334 ± 0.007 µm/min.
source: In time-lapse movies of DMSO-treated embryos, myocardial cells display coherent medially directed movement (Figure 3A–B, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–A''', Figure 3—video 1) with an average velocity of 0.2334 ± 0.007 µm/min, which is consistent with previous studies (Holtzman et al., 2007; Bloomekatz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A–B, E and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: In PI3K-inhibited embryos myocardial cells display coherent, coordinated movement and do move in the general direction of the midline, however they make dramatically less progress.
source: In PI3K-inhibited embryos myocardial cells also display coherent, coordinated movement and do move in the general direction of the midline, however they make dramatically less progress (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–B''', Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–B'''.

claim: Myocardial cells in PI3K-inhibited embryos are slower (0.1879 ± 0.008 µm/min) and less efficient.
source: Quantitative analysis of these myocardial cell tracks reveals that myocardial cells are slower (0.1879 ± 0.008 µm/min) and less efficient (Figure 3E, F, Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell tracks shown in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Differences in speed between DMSO- and LY-treated embryos occur throughout cardiac fusion.
source: A close analysis of the differences in speed found that they occur throughout cardiac fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and are mostly due to defective movement along the medial–lateral axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) rather than defects in angular movement occurring along the anterior–posterior axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Differences in speed between DMSO- and LY-treated embryos are mostly due to defective movement along the medial–lateral axis rather than defects in angular movement occurring along the anterior–posterior axis.
source: A close analysis of the differences in speed found that they occur throughout cardiac fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and are mostly due to defective movement along the medial–lateral axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) rather than defects in angular movement occurring along the anterior–posterior axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: Tracks of myocardial cells in DMSO-treated embryos are predominately oriented in a medial direction (average of 31.1 ± 1.65°).
source: Tracks of myocardial cells in DMSO-treated embryos are predominately oriented in a medial direction (average of 31.1 ± 1.65°), while tracks in LY-treated embryos are mostly oriented in an angular anterior direction (60.6 ± 1.73°, p-value = 2.77 × 10−12, Figure 3G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: Tracks of myocardial cells in LY-treated embryos are mostly oriented in an angular anterior direction (60.6 ± 1.73°).
source: Tracks of myocardial cells in DMSO-treated embryos are predominately oriented in a medial direction (average of 31.1 ± 1.65°), while tracks in LY-treated embryos are mostly oriented in an angular anterior direction (60.6 ± 1.73°, p-value = 2.77 × 10−12, Figure 3G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G, H.

claim: Differences in direction of movement between DMSO- and LY-treated embryos occur mainly in the early stages of cardiac fusion when wild-type myocardial movement is mostly medial.
source: These differences occur mainly in the early stages of cardiac fusion when wild-type myocardial movement is mostly medial (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: PI3K signaling is responsible for both steering and propelling myocardial cells toward the midline.
source: Altogether, this analysis of myocardial cell tracks suggests that PI3K signaling is responsible for both steering and propelling myocardial cells toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of myocardial cell tracks showing defects in both direction and speed.

claim: The lateral edges of myocardial cells in wild-type/DMSO-treated embryos are highly dynamic; transitioning from appearing smooth and coherent to undulating and extending finger-like membrane protrusions away from the cell.
source: Despite myocardial cells being connected via intercellular junctions (Trinh and Stainier, 2004; Bloomekatz et al., 2017), we observed that the lateral edges of myocardial cells in wild-type/DMSO-treated embryos are highly dynamic; transitioning from appearing smooth and coherent to undulating and extending finger-like membrane protrusions away from the cell (Figure 4A–A'''', Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A–A''''.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions actively extend and retract.
source: These protrusions actively extend and retract, and are prevalent occurring on average 20.3 ± 6.7 times per hour per cell and lasting for an average of 2.3 ± 0.6 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions occur on average 20.3 ± 6.7 times per hour per cell in DMSO-treated embryos.
source: These protrusions actively extend and retract, and are prevalent occurring on average 20.3 ± 6.7 times per hour per cell and lasting for an average of 2.3 ± 0.6 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions last for an average of 2.3 ± 0.6 min in DMSO-treated embryos.
source: These protrusions actively extend and retract, and are prevalent occurring on average 20.3 ± 6.7 times per hour per cell and lasting for an average of 2.3 ± 0.6 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Different types of protrusion morphologies were observed, including thin finger-like protrusions and wide protrusions which have a wider base.
source: We observed different types of protrusion morphologies, including thin finger-like protrusions and wide protrusions which have a wider base (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In LY-treated embryos, similar types of membrane protrusions extend from myocardial cells.
source: In LY-treated embryos we observed similar types of membrane protrusions extending from myocardial cells (Figure 4B–B'''', Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4B–B''''.

claim: Membrane protrusions in LY-treated embryos occur at a similar rate to those found in DMSO-treated embryos (17 ± 7.4 per hour per cell, p-value = 0.36).
source: These protrusions occur at a similar rate to those found in DMSO-treated embryos (17 ± 7.4 per hour per cell, p-value = 0.36), but with slightly longer persistence (3.23 ± 0.84 min, p-value = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Membrane protrusions in LY-treated embryos have slightly longer persistence (3.23 ± 0.84 min, p-value = 0.008) compared to DMSO-treated embryos.
source: These protrusions occur at a similar rate to those found in DMSO-treated embryos (17 ± 7.4 per hour per cell, p-value = 0.36), but with slightly longer persistence (3.23 ± 0.84 min, p-value = 0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Both types of membrane protrusions in DMSO-treated embryos occur predominantly in the medial direction (77.25 ± 21.76% of protrusions were in the forward/medial direction).
source: We further observed that both types of membrane protrusions in DMSO-treated embryos occur predominantly in the medial direction (77.25 ± 21.76% of protrusions were in the forward/medial direction, Figure 4A–A'''', C, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D), suggesting an association with the medial movement of the myocardial tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In LY-treated embryos myocardial membrane protrusions do not display the same medial polarity, instead extending from all sides of a myocardial cell equally (only 46 ± 11.6% of protrusion were in the forward direction).
source: In contrast, in LY-treated embryos myocardial membrane protrusions do not display the same medial polarity, instead extending from all sides of a myocardial cell equally (only 46 ± 11.6% of protrusion were in the forward direction, Figure 4B–B'''', C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: PI3K signaling helps to steer and propel myocardial cells toward the midline through the polarization of active protrusions.
source: The finding that myocardial membrane protrusions are medially polarized in wild-type embryos but not in PI3K-inhibited embryos where myocardial cells are misdirected and slower to reach the midline suggests that PI3K signaling helps to steer and propel myocardial cells toward the midline through the polarization of these active protrusions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that protrusions are polarized in wild-type but not in PI3K-inhibited embryos.

claim: PI3K activity as measured by the ratio of phospho-AKT to AKT levels is severely diminished in pdgfra mutant embryos during cardiac fusion.
source: We found that PI3K activity as measured by the ratio of phospho-AKT to AKT levels (Alessi et al., 1996) is severely diminished in pdgfra mutant embryos during cardiac fusion (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When Pdgfra activity is increased during cardiac fusion through the over-expression of pdgfaa, PI3K activity is upregulated.
source: Conversely, when Pdgfra activity is increased during cardiac fusion through the over-expression of pdgfaa, PI3K activity is upregulated (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When pdgfra heterozygous mutant embryos are exposed to DMSO cardiac fusion occurs normally.
source: When pdgfra heterozygous mutant embryos are exposed to DMSO cardiac fusion occurs normally (Figure 5D, F), even though there is a small reduction in PI3K activity (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D, F.

claim: In wild-type embryos exposed to 10 μM LY, PI3K activity is modestly reduced and a small percent of embryos display mild cardiac fusion defects (average of 10.9 ± 7.39% of 10 μM LY-treated embryos display mild U-shaped cardiac fusion defects).
source: Similarly, in wild-type embryos exposed to 10 μM LY, PI3K activity is modestly reduced (Figure 1H) and a small percent of embryos display mild cardiac fusion defects (average of 10.9 ± 7.39% of 10 μM LY-treated embryos display mild U-shaped cardiac fusion defects, n = 36, 3 replicates, Figure 5C, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 5C, F.

claim: When pdgfra heterozygous mutant embryos are exposed to 10 μM LY, there is a synergistic increase in both the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion defects.
source: However, when pdgfra heterozygous mutant embryos are exposed to 10 μM LY, there is a synergistic increase in both the severity and penetrance of cardiac fusion defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased defects in the double perturbation.

claim: 100% of pdgfra heterozygous embryos exposed to 10 μM LY display cardiac fusion defects, with the majority of embryos displaying severe cardia bifida phenotypes.
source: 100% of pdgfra heterozygous embryos exposed to 10 μM LY display cardiac fusion defects, with the majority of embryos displaying severe cardia bifida phenotypes (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Cardiac fusion defects caused by exogenous expression of pdgfaa could be rescued by a sub-phenotypic reduction in PI3K activity.
source: Furthermore, we found that cardiac fusion defects caused by exogenous expression of pdgfaa (Figure 5H, J, Bloomekatz et al., 2017), which causes increased PI3K activity (Figure 5B), could be rescued by a sub-phenotypic reduction in PI3K activity (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5H, I, J.

claim: PDGF signaling activates PI3K activity to promote myocardial movement toward the midline.
source: Together these results suggest that PDGF signaling activates PI3K activity to promote myocardial movement toward the midline.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the genetic interaction data and biochemical measurements.

claim: Pdgfra in the myocardium senses signals (PDGF ligands) from the endoderm and via the PI3K pathway directs myocardial movement toward the midline through the production of medially oriented membrane protrusions.
source: Together with our previous studies revealing a role for the PDGF pathway in facilitating communication between the endoderm and myocardium (Bloomekatz et al., 2017), our current work suggests a model in which Pdgfra in the myocardium senses signals (PDGF ligands) from the endoderm and via the PI3K pathway directs myocardial movement toward the midline through the production of medially oriented membrane protrusions.
evidence: The claim is a model that integrates current findings with prior work.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions during cardiac fusion were postulated by De Haan et al. in 1967 as a mechanism by which myocardial cells move toward the midline.
source: Myocardial membrane protrusions during cardiac fusion were postulated by De Haan et al. in 1967 as a mechanism by which myocardial cells move toward the midline (DeHaan, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (DeHaan, 1967).

claim: Previous studies in zebrafish observed myocardial protrusions prior to and after cardiac fusion.
source: These studies are complemented by previous studies in zebrafish which observed myocardial protrusions prior to and after cardiac fusion (Ye et al., 2015; Rohr et al., 2008) as well as recent studies in the mice (Dominguez et al., 2023) indicating that these cellular processes are likely conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ye et al., 2015; Rohr et al., 2008).

claim: Recent studies in mice observed myocardial protrusions indicating that these cellular processes are likely conserved.
source: These studies are complemented by previous studies in zebrafish which observed myocardial protrusions prior to and after cardiac fusion (Ye et al., 2015; Rohr et al., 2008) as well as recent studies in the mice (Dominguez et al., 2023) indicating that these cellular processes are likely conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent work (Dominguez et al., 2023) and is an inference about conservation.

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during trabeculation.
source: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during trabeculation (Staudt et al., 2014), cardiac regeneration (Morikawa et al., 2015; Aharonov et al., 2020) and during the muscularization of the outflow tract (van den Hoff et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Staudt et al., 2014).

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during cardiac regeneration.
source: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during trabeculation (Staudt et al., 2014), cardiac regeneration (Morikawa et al., 2015; Aharonov et al., 2020) and during the muscularization of the outflow tract (van den Hoff et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Morikawa et al., 2015; Aharonov et al., 2020).

claim: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during the muscularization of the outflow tract.
source: Myocardial membrane protrusions have been discovered during trabeculation (Staudt et al., 2014), cardiac regeneration (Morikawa et al., 2015; Aharonov et al., 2020) and during the muscularization of the outflow tract (van den Hoff et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (van den Hoff et al., 1999).

claim: PI3K signaling orients and stimulates protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells.
source: Indeed, similar observations of PI3K signaling orienting and stimulating protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells as well as in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells, the prechordal plate, and the dorsal epithelium (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2003; Garlena et al., 2015; Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008) support a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010).

claim: PI3K signaling orients and stimulates protrusion formation in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells.
source: Indeed, similar observations of PI3K signaling orienting and stimulating protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells as well as in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells, the prechordal plate, and the dorsal epithelium (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2003; Garlena et al., 2015; Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008) support a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008).

claim: PI3K signaling orients and stimulates protrusion formation in the collective movement of the prechordal plate.
source: Indeed, similar observations of PI3K signaling orienting and stimulating protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells as well as in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells, the prechordal plate, and the dorsal epithelium (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2003; Garlena et al., 2015; Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008) support a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Montero et al., 2003).

claim: PI3K signaling orients and stimulates protrusion formation in the collective movement of the dorsal epithelium.
source: Indeed, similar observations of PI3K signaling orienting and stimulating protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells as well as in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells, the prechordal plate, and the dorsal epithelium (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2003; Garlena et al., 2015; Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008) support a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Garlena et al., 2015).

claim: There is a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
source: Indeed, similar observations of PI3K signaling orienting and stimulating protrusion formation in migrating Dictyostelium and neutrophil cells as well as in the collective movement of endothelial tip cells, the prechordal plate, and the dorsal epithelium (Iijima and Devreotes, 2002; Yoo et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2003; Garlena et al., 2015; Dumortier et al., 2012; Graupera et al., 2008) support a conserved role for PI3K signaling in regulating protrusion formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on observations across multiple systems cited.

claim: Directionality and to a lesser extent velocity and efficiency are compromised when membrane protrusions are improperly oriented in PI3K-inhibited embryos.
source: Our studies indicate that directionality and to a lesser extent velocity and efficiency are compromised, when membrane protrusions are improperly oriented in PI3K-inhibited embryos (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed membrane protrusions could be force generating, similar to protrusions from leader cells in the lateral line or in endothelial and tracheal tip cells.
source: These observations could suggest that the observed membrane protrusions are force generating, similar to protrusions from leader cells in the lateral line or in endothelial and tracheal tip cells (Caussinus et al., 2008; Dalle Nogare et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by citations to analogous systems.

claim: The observed membrane protrusions could act more like filopodia sensing extrinsic signals and the extracellular environment.
source: Alternatively, these protrusions could act more like filopodia sensing extrinsic signals and the extracellular environment (Heckman and Plummer, 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: A similar Pdgfra–PI3K signaling cassette is important in the collective directional migration of several organ progenitors including the migration of mesoderm and neural crest cells.
source: Indeed, a similar Pdgfra–PI3K signaling cassette is important in the collective directional migration of several organ progenitors including the migration of mesoderm and neural crest cells (Montero et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2008; McCarthy et al., 2013; Bahm et al., 2017; Symes and Mercola, 1996; Klinghoffer et al., 2002; He and Soriano, 2013; Nagel and Winklbauer, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: RTK–PI3K pathways are important across several cardiac developmental processes, including epicardial development, cardiac neural crest addition, cardiomyocyte growth, cardiac fibroblast movement, and cardiomyocyte contraction.
source: RTK–PI3K pathways are also important across several cardiac developmental processes, including epicardial development, cardiac neural crest addition, cardiomyocyte growth, cardiac fibroblast movement, and cardiomyocyte contraction (Crackower et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2010; Sato et al., 2011; Ivey et al., 2019; McMullen et al., 2003; Shioi et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: PDGF–PI3K and more generally RTK–PI3K signaling cassettes are activated in several diseases including glioblastomas, gastrointestinal stromal tumors, and cardiac fibrosis.
source: Similarly, PDGF–PI3K and more generally RTK–PI3K signaling cassettes are activated in several diseases including glioblastomas, gastrointestinal stromal tumors, and cardiac fibrosis (Wang et al., 1997; Cheng et al., 2009; Fan et al., 2014; Lennartsson et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The role of the RTK–PI3K cassette in sensing and responding to extracellular signals is likely to be broadly relevant to the etiology of a wide array of developmental processes as well as congenital diseases.
source: Thus, the role of this RTK–PI3K cassette in sensing and responding to extracellular signals is likely to be broadly relevant to the etiology of a wide array of developmental processes as well as congenital diseases.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the broad involvement of RTK–PI3K signaling in multiple contexts.
